lessonTitle: Mean Effective Pressure and Engine Power

blocks.text: Two engines are advertised: a 1.0 L three-cylinder turbo petrol producing 90 kW and a 5.0 L naturally aspirated V8 producing 280 kW. Which one makes better use of its cylinders? Power alone cannot say, because the V8 is five times larger. The mean effective pressure scales out engine size and speed, so it is the engineer's fair comparison of how hard each cycle works its cylinder volume.

blocks.markdown: An engine produces work by repeated cycles. In one cycle the gas does a net work $W_{net}$ on the piston, equal to the area enclosed by the $p$-$V$ diagram. The cylinder volume swept by the piston is the **displacement volume** $V_d = V_{max} - V_{min}$. If all the net work were delivered at a constant pressure over the stroke, what pressure would give the same work? That pressure is the **mean effective pressure**.

blocks.title: Mean effective pressure (mep)
blocks.text: The constant pressure which, acting on the piston over the displacement volume, would produce the same net work as the actual cycle. It is an average over the stroke, not a peak pressure. Subscripts: $i$ = indicated (from the gas pressures in the cylinder), $b$ = brake (from measured output at the shaft).

blocks.caption: Units: $W_{net}$ in J (or kJ) and $V_d$ in m³ give mep in Pa (or kPa). 1 MPa = $10^6$ J/m³.

$V_d$ is the total displacement of all cylinders (m³); $N$ is shaft speed in revolutions per second; $\dot W_i$ in W. A four-stroke engine completes one power cycle every two revolutions, which gives the factor of 1/2.

blocks.title: Mep and indicated power
blocks.prompt: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine has a displacement of 0.5 L (0.5 × 10⁻³ m³) per cylinder. Each cylinder does a net work of 600 J per cycle. The engine runs at 3000 rev/min. Find the indicated mep and the indicated power.

steps.text: Mep from net work and displacement per cylinder.
Total displacement and speed in revolutions per second.

blocks.answer: imep = 1.20 MPa and indicated power = 60.0 kW. Check: 4 cylinders × 600 J × 25 power cycles/s = 60.0 kW.

blocks.title: Why mep is useful
blocks.text: Power equals mep × displacement × speed (with the $n_R$ factor). At equal mep, a larger or faster engine gives proportionately more power. Mep therefore measures how effectively the cylinder volume is used, independent of engine size and speed: naturally aspirated petrol engines typically have bmep in the range of about 0.8 to 1.2 MPa, and turbocharged diesels reach 1.5 to 2 MPa (typical values).

blocks.markdown: The pressure in the cylinder is measured to find the indicated work, so indicated quantities describe the gas cycle alone. Friction between piston rings and cylinder, bearings, valve train and engine-driven pumps and fans consume some indicated power before the shaft delivers it. The power available at the output shaft, measured by a dynamometer, is the **brake power**.

blocks.latex: \dot W_b = \eta_m\,\dot W_i \qquad \dot W_f = \dot W_i - \dot W_b \qquad \eta_m = \frac{\dot W_b}{\dot W_i} = \frac{\mathrm{bmep}}{\mathrm{imep}}
blocks.caption: Mechanical efficiency $\eta_m$ is typically 0.75 to 0.9 at full load. Friction power $\dot W_f$ is the loss between the cylinder and the shaft.

blocks.title: Brake power and mechanical efficiency
blocks.prompt: The engine of the previous example delivers a brake power of 48 kW at 3000 rev/min. Find the mechanical efficiency, friction power and brake mean effective pressure.

steps.text: Mechanical efficiency from brake and indicated power.
Brake mep by rearranging the power equation, $\mathrm{bmep} = \dot W_b\,n_R/(V_d N)$.

blocks.answer: ηm = 0.800, friction power = 12.0 kW, bmep = 960 kPa (= ηm × imep).

rows: Roughly independent of load, rises with speed
blocks.caption: Engine performance measures.

items: At part load $\dot W_i$ falls but friction stays nearly constant, so $\eta_m$ falls (at idle $\dot W_b = 0$ and $\eta_m = 0$).
Two-stroke engines have a power stroke every revolution: $n_R = 1$.
Brake torque and brake power are related by $\dot W_b = T\omega = 2\pi N T$ ($N$ in rev/s).
Mep has units of pressure but is not a pressure measured at any point; it is a work-per-volume average.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Convert rev/min to rev/s before using the formula. Use total displacement for total power, per-cylinder displacement for per-cylinder work. Do not forget $n_R = 2$ for a four-stroke engine. Keep J/m³ = Pa straight when computing mep.

points: $\mathrm{mep} = W_{net}/V_d$: the constant pressure that gives the same work.
$\dot W_b = \eta_m \dot W_i$ and the friction power is $\dot W_i - \dot W_b$.
Mep allows engines of different sizes and speeds to be compared fairly.

questions.stem: The mean effective pressure of an engine is defined as

options.text: the peak cylinder pressure averaged over many cycles
the pressure at the exhaust valve during blowdown
the net work per cycle divided by the displacement volume
the net work per cycle divided by the clearance volume

questions.correctOptionText: the net work per cycle divided by the displacement volume

distractorRationale.a: Mep is a work-based average, not a peak pressure.
distractorRationale.d: The displacement volume is used, not the clearance volume.

questions.explanation: Mep is the constant pressure that, acting through the displacement volume, would give the same net work as the real cycle. It is $W_{net}/V_d$, which lets different engines be compared on a per-volume basis.

questions.stem: A dynamometer measures a brake power of 60 kW and a pressure transducer analysis gives an indicated power of 75 kW. What is the friction power?

options.text: 15 kW
135 kW
0.8 kW
60 kW

distractorRationale.b: Adds the two powers instead of subtracting.
distractorRationale.c: This is the mechanical efficiency written as a number, not a power.
distractorRationale.d: This is the brake power itself.

questions.explanation: Friction power is the difference $\dot W_f = \dot W_i - \dot W_b = 75 - 60 = 15$ kW. The mechanical efficiency is $60/75 = 0.80$.

questions.stem: A four-stroke engine runs at a constant indicated mep. If the speed is doubled, what happens to the indicated power (neglecting changes in breathing)?

options.text: It stays the same
It quadruples
It halves
It doubles

distractorRationale.a: Power is proportional to speed at fixed mep.
distractorRationale.b: Power is linear, not quadratic, in speed.
distractorRationale.c: Power rises with speed at fixed mep.

questions.explanation: Indicated power is $\mathrm{imep}\,V_d\,N/n_R$, so at fixed imep it is proportional to the speed $N$. In practice mep falls at high speed as breathing worsens.

questions.stem: Why does the mechanical efficiency of a car engine fall at part load?

options.text: Friction power rises sharply as the throttle closes
Friction power is nearly constant while the indicated power drops
Indicated power increases at part load
Mechanical efficiency does not depend on load

questions.correctOptionText: Friction power is nearly constant while the indicated power drops

distractorRationale.c: Indicated power decreases at part load.
distractorRationale.d: It does, because of the nearly constant friction.

questions.explanation: Since $\eta_m = (\dot W_i - \dot W_f)/\dot W_i$ and $\dot W_f$ is almost constant at fixed speed, a smaller $\dot W_i$ gives a lower $\eta_m$. At idle all the indicated power goes into friction.

questions.stem: Engine X has a 1.5 L displacement and Engine Y has a 3.0 L displacement. Both operate at a bmep of 1.0 MPa and the same speed. How does the brake power compare, for the same type (four-stroke) of engine?

options.text: They produce the same brake power because the bmep is the same
Engine X produces twice the brake power of engine Y
Engine Y produces twice the brake power of engine X
Engine Y produces four times the brake power

questions.correctOptionText: Engine Y produces twice the brake power of engine X

distractorRationale.d: Power is proportional to displacement, not its square.

questions.explanation: Brake power $= \mathrm{bmep}\,V_d N/n_R$, so at equal bmep and speed it is proportional to displacement. The 3.0 L engine therefore produces twice as much.

questions.stem: A single cylinder produces a net work of 420 J per cycle with a displacement volume of 0.40 L (0.40 × 10⁻³ m³). Calculate the indicated mean effective pressure in kPa.
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{imep} = W_{net}/V_d = 420/(0.40\times10^{-3}) = 1050000$ Pa $= 1050$ kPa. The result is quoted in kPa and is of a physically reasonable magnitude.

questions.stem: A three-cylinder four-stroke engine has a displacement of 0.33 L per cylinder and an indicated mep of 0.95 MPa. At 5400 rev/min, calculate the indicated power in kW.
questions.explanation: Total $V_d = 3\times0.33\times10^{-3} = 0.99\times10^{-3}$ m³ and $N = 5400/60 = 90$ rev/s. Then $\dot W_i = 0.95\times10^{6}\times0.99\times10^{-3}\times90/2 = 42322$ W $= 42.32$ kW.

questions.stem: A single-cylinder two-stroke engine has a displacement of 0.125 L, an indicated mep of 0.55 MPa and a mechanical efficiency of 0.78. At 6000 rev/min, calculate the brake power in kW.
questions.explanation: For a two-stroke $n_R = 1$ and $N = 100$ rev/s, so $\dot W_i = 0.55\times10^{6}\times0.125\times10^{-3}\times100 = 6875$ W. Brake power $= 0.78\times6.875 = 5.362$ kW.

questions.stem: Explain why mean effective pressure is a better measure than power for comparing the performance of two engines of different size, and state what it does not tell you.
markingGuide: Mep $= W_{net}/V_d$, the work per unit displaced volume
Power scales with displacement and speed, so a larger or faster engine gives more power trivially
Mep removes the effect of size and speed, giving a measure of how effectively the cylinder volume is used
Higher mep indicates better use of the cylinder (e.g. boosting, better combustion, good breathing)
Does not tell the efficiency (fuel use) or the peak pressure or cost
Mentions indicated vs brake: bmep includes friction losses
questions.explanation: Mep is work per unit displacement, so it measures how hard the cylinder volume is worked regardless of size and speed. It says nothing about fuel economy or peak stresses.

questions.stem: A 3.0 L four-stroke engine at 4000 rev/min has an indicated mep of 1.3 MPa and delivers 100 kW of brake power. (a) Calculate the indicated power. (b) Find the mechanical efficiency and friction power. (c) Calculate the brake mep and explain what it represents.
markingGuide: Brake mep $= \dot W_b n_R/(V_d N) = 1000$ kPa (equal to $\eta_m \times$ imep)
Explains bmep as the average pressure equivalent to the useful work at the shaft per unit displacement
Correct unit handling (rev/min to rev/s, factor 2 for four-stroke)
questions.explanation: Indicated power is 130.0 kW, so $\eta_m = 0.769$ and the friction power is 30.0 kW. Brake mep is 1000 kPa, the pressure that would give the delivered shaft work over the displacement volume.
